resources.string: Telemetry and control for your ESP32 projects
Common problems and how to fix them. Tap a problem to see the solution.
ESP32-BT does not appear when scanning

Power on the ESP32 and press RESET. In Arduino IDE, open Serial Monitor at 115200 baud and confirm it prints ESP32 Bluetooth Receiver Ready. On the app Bluetooth screen, tap refresh to scan, move closer to the ESP32, and stop scanning when ESP32-BT appears in Scanned Devices.

Open Bluetooth from Home, start a scan, and tap ESP32-BT. If it was paired before, try Paired Devices instead. If connection still fails, forget ESP32-BT in Android system Bluetooth settings, scan again, and pair from Scanned Devices.

Only one phone should control the ESP32 at a time. Close other apps that may use the Bluetooth link. Open Bluetooth from Home, connect to ESP32-BT, and wait until the Bluetooth card shows Connected before opening RC Control.
RC sticks, switches, or buttons have no effect

Connect over Bluetooth first (Home must show Connected). Open RC Control in landscape. Confirm the ESP32 sketch is uploaded and Serial Monitor shows ESP32 Bluetooth Receiver Ready. Test inputs with Serial Monitor debug enabled as shown in the Tutorial.
Gauges, LEDs, seven-segment displays, or plot do not update

Telemetry is sent by the ESP32 firmware. Stay on the RC Control screen with Bluetooth connected. Reflash the sketch if needed and verify debug_config.h and telemetry settings. Use the Tutorial telemetry test steps to confirm the firmware is sending data.
First-time setup — where do I start?

Follow the in-app Tutorial in order: get the ESP32 ZIP from Codes and Documents, upload ESP32_BT_Controller.ino in Arduino IDE, connect via Bluetooth, configure RC Settings, then open RC Control. The Help button is always available from Home for quick troubleshooting.

Match the blue numbered badges on the Home screen image (1–6) to the items below.

1. Quick Start (bottom): reconnects to the last saved Bluetooth device, or sends you to scan for a new device.

2. Control modules: opens the module catalog (Control panel, Smart home, and more). Tap a module to open it.

3. Bluetooth: opens the device list to scan, connect, and check the current connection status.

4. Codes and Documents: opens PDF guides and lets you share or save the ESP32_BT_Controller-main.zip code file.

5. Tutorial: opens this step-by-step app guide.

6. Help (top-right): shortcut for quick troubleshooting tips.

This video shows how to prepare the ESP32 in Arduino IDE:

- Open ESP32_BT_Controller.ino in Arduino IDE (download the ZIP from the app in step 2 if you do not have the sketch yet).

- Select the correct ESP32 board under Tools > Board.

- Select the serial port connected to your ESP32 under Tools > Port.

- Upload the sketch to the ESP32.

- Open Tools > Serial Monitor and set the baud rate to 115200.

- Press the ESP32 RESET button.

- Confirm the monitor prints: ESP32 Bluetooth Receiver Ready.

- When you see that message, the ESP32 is waiting for a Bluetooth connection from the app (step 4).

This video shows how to get the project files from the app:

- Open Codes and Documents on the Home screen and tap the ESP32 BT Controller ZIP item.

- Choose Share or send to email or messaging, or Save to Downloads to keep a copy on the phone.

- Open the ZIP where you saved it or from the app you shared to.

- Extract the archive if needed and locate ESP32_BT_Controller.ino.

- Transfer the folder to your computer if you uploaded from the phone, then continue with step 3 in Arduino IDE.
Connect to the ESP32 with Bluetooth

This GIF shows how to connect the app to the ESP32-BT device:

- From the Home screen, tap the Bluetooth button.

- On the Bluetooth screen, tap the refresh icon in the top app bar to start scanning.

- When ESP32-BT appears, tap the X icon to stop scanning.

- Check the Scanned Devices list and find ESP32-BT.

- If this is the first connection, tap ESP32-BT from Scanned Devices to pair and connect.

- If the ESP32 was already paired before, tap ESP32-BT from Paired Devices to connect faster.

- After the connection succeeds, the app returns to the Home screen.

- Confirm that the Bluetooth button now shows the Connected status.

This video shows how to review and apply the controller settings:

- From the Home screen (Bluetooth Connected), tap Control modules.

- Open Control panel, then tap the settings icon in the top bar to open Control panel settings.

- On RC Controller Settings, review Joystick Settings and choose the behavior for the left and right sticks.

- Review Initial Switch Positions and set the starting state for switches S1 to S6.

- Review Initial Knob Values and set the starting value for the left and right knobs.

- Return to the Home screen after the configuration is saved.

- Tap Control modules again, then tap Control panel to open the controller.

- Confirm that joystick behavior, switch states, and knob values are applied correctly on the RC screen.

The RC Control screen runs in landscape. The numbers on the image match this list:

1. Header indicators — Left: analog gauge with integer value and title from ESP32 telemetry. Right: battery-style level and title from telemetry. Both update when the firmware sends new indicator data.

2. Seven-segment displays — Left and right numeric panels (for example RPM). Each has its own title, color, and on/off state from firmware telemetry.

3. Status LEDs — Four LEDs on each side (eight total). Left uses the lower four bits of the LED byte; right uses the upper four. Each LED lights when its bit is set in incoming telemetry.

4. Joysticks — Left and right 3D sticks. Drag to send X and Y in the control packet. Return behavior (spring, hold, etc.) is set per side under Joystick Settings in RC Controller Settings.

5. Switches (S1–S6) — Three toggles on the left (S1–S3) and three on the right (S4–S6). Each maps to a bit in the switch byte; initial on/off states are configured in settings.

6. Rotary knobs — Left and right knobs. Turn to set a 0–100% style auxiliary value sent continuously to the ESP32.

7. Action buttons — Four momentary buttons (upper and lower on each side). Press to send one-shot event packets: CENTER_TOP_LEFT, CENTER_BOTTOM_LEFT, CENTER_TOP_RIGHT, and CENTER_BOTTOM_RIGHT.

8. Center telemetry plot — Live graph area fed by Bluetooth plot series from the ESP32.

While this screen is open, control packets are sent continuously. Connect over Bluetooth before opening RC Control so telemetry and inputs stay in sync with the ESP32.

This video tests every RC screen component from step 6 while the Arduino IDE Serial Monitor runs at 115200 baud next to the app.

Setup before recording:

- In `debug_config.h`, set `DEBUG_ENABLED` to 1 and enable `DBG_STICKS`, `DBG_KNOBS`, `DBG_SWITCHES`, and `DBG_EVENTS`. If your firmware exposes telemetry debug (panels, LEDs, indicators, or plot), enable that too. Reflash the ESP32.

- Connect the phone to the ESP32 over Bluetooth, open RC Control, and open Serial Monitor in the Arduino IDE.

What the video should show (same order as step 6):

1. Header indicators — Change analog and battery values from the firmware (or your test sketch). On the app, the left gauge and right battery indicator update. In Serial Monitor, confirm the matching indicator or telemetry debug lines your firmware prints.

2. Seven-segment displays — Update left and right panel values from the firmware. Both numeric panels on the app should follow. Serial Monitor should show the panel or telemetry output your sketch uses.

3. Status LEDs — Change the LED byte from the firmware. All eight LEDs on the app should follow the lower and upper four bits. Confirm the LED or telemetry lines in Serial Monitor.

4. Joysticks — Move the left stick, then the right. Serial Monitor should print `L Stick X:` / `L Stick Y:` and `R Stick X:` / `R Stick Y:` updating roughly in the 0 to 1023 range with center near 512.

5. Switches (S1–S6) — Toggle every switch. Expect `Switch Byte:` plus lines such as `S1 = ON` or `S4 = OFF` for each change.

6. Rotary knobs — Turn the left and right knobs. Expect `Left Knob:` and `Right Knob:` values to track each movement.

7. Action buttons — Press the upper and lower button on each side. Each press should print an event dump such as `--- EVENT PACKET (PRESS) ---` with the event id and checksum.

8. Center telemetry plot — Send plot series from the firmware. The center graph on the app should scroll or update. Confirm plot or telemetry debug in Serial Monitor if your firmware prints it.

When finished, center both joysticks and return switches and knobs to a safe default before driving hardware.

This video shows how to drive the left and right seven-segment displays on the RC screen (step 6, item 2) using test values typed in the Arduino IDE Serial Monitor.

Firmware setup before recording:

- Open `debug_config.h` in the ESP32 project.

- Set `DEBUG_ENABLED` to 1.

- Set `#define TELEMETRY_DEBUG_MODE DBG_PANEL` so the firmware accepts panel test values over Serial Monitor.

- Upload the sketch to the ESP32 and wait until it is running.

App and Serial Monitor setup:

- Connect the phone to the ESP32 over Bluetooth.

- Open RC Control on the app so both seven-segment panels are visible.

- In the Arduino IDE, open Serial Monitor at 115200 baud.

What the video should show:

- The firmware prompts for panel values (or you send them as your sketch defines).

- Type a first test value, for example `100`, and confirm the left seven-segment display on the RC screen updates to show it.

- Type a second test value, for example `200`, and confirm the right seven-segment display updates to show it.

- Serial Monitor should echo or confirm the values the ESP32 sends over Bluetooth telemetry.

- Optionally change the values again to show both panels tracking new numbers in real time.

If the panels do not update, verify Bluetooth is connected, `TELEMETRY_DEBUG_MODE` is `DBG_PANEL`, and the app is on the RC Control screen.
Test analog, battery, and LED telemetry

This video shows how to test the left analog indicator, the right battery indicator, and the LED-style boolean status LEDs on the RC screen (step 6, items 1 and 3) using values sent from the Arduino IDE Serial Monitor.

Firmware setup before recording:

- Open `debug_config.h` in the ESP32 project.

- Set `DEBUG_ENABLED` to 1.

- Set `#define TELEMETRY_DEBUG_MODE DBG_INDICATOR` so the firmware accepts indicator and LED test values over Serial Monitor.

- Upload the sketch to the ESP32 and wait until it is running.

App and Serial Monitor setup:

- Connect the phone to the ESP32 over Bluetooth.

- Open RC Control on the app so the header indicators and status LEDs on both sides are visible.

- In the Arduino IDE, open Serial Monitor at 115200 baud.

What the video should show:

- The firmware prompts for three test inputs (or you send them as your sketch defines).

- Enter an analog test value (for example `75`) and confirm the left analog gauge on the RC screen updates.

- Enter a battery test value (for example `90`) and confirm the right battery indicator updates.

- Enter the LED-style boolean indicator values (for example a pattern such as `1,0,1,0` or the format your firmware expects) and confirm the status LEDs on the RC screen turn on and off to match.

- Serial Monitor should echo or confirm the telemetry the ESP32 sends over Bluetooth for each input.

- Optionally change the three values again to show all indicators tracking in real time.

If nothing updates on the app, verify Bluetooth is connected, `TELEMETRY_DEBUG_MODE` is `DBG_INDICATOR`, and the app is on the RC Control screen.

This video shows how plot channel labels are defined in firmware and how three plot test values sent from the Arduino IDE Serial Monitor drive the center telemetry graph on the RC screen (step 6, item 8).

Part 1 — Plot labels in `telemetry.cpp`:

- Open `telemetry.cpp` in the ESP32 project and locate `sendConfigTelemetry()`.

- In the CONFIG LABELS section, show the `plotNames[]` array (for example `"Volts"`, `"Amps"`, `"RPMs"`). These strings are sent once over Bluetooth after connect and become the legend labels in the app plot.

- Optionally point out `panelNames[]` (`"Left"`, `"Right"`) and `indicatorNames[]` (`"Throttle"`, `"Battery"`) in the same function for panel and header titles.

- Upload the sketch after any label changes.

Part 2 — Plot value test over Serial Monitor:

- In `debug_config.h`, set `DEBUG_ENABLED` to 1.

- Set `#define TELEMETRY_DEBUG_MODE DBG_PLOT` so the firmware reads three plot test values from Serial Monitor (`getPlot1()`, `getPlot2()`, `getPlot3()`).

- Reflash the ESP32, connect the phone over Bluetooth, and open RC Control so the center graph and legend are visible.

- Open Serial Monitor at 115200 baud. After Bluetooth connects, confirm `Telemetry config sent...` appears when `sendConfigTelemetry()` runs.

What the video should show:

- Enter three plot test values (for example `120`, `80`, and `200` in the format your firmware expects).

- The ESP32 sends plot packets (`0xCC 0x33` header) about every 50 ms with those three bytes.

- On the RC screen, the legend lists Volts, Amps, and RPMs and the real-time graph traces update for all three channels.

- Change the three values in Serial Monitor again to show the graph following the new levels.

If labels are wrong, edit `plotNames[]` in `telemetry.cpp` and reconnect so config is sent again. If the graph stays flat, verify Bluetooth, `TELEMETRY_DEBUG_MODE` is `DBG_PLOT`, and the RC Control screen is open.
Telemetry and control for ESP32 over Bluetooth
TeleCon4ESP32 connects your phone to ESP32 hardware over Bluetooth. Control sticks, switches, knobs, and view live telemetry from your firmware.
How we handle Bluetooth, local settings, and ads

Bluetooth: device discovery, pairing, and live control/telemetry with hardware you connect — not sent to MICSBOL servers.

Local storage: last device and RC settings on your phone only.

Ads: Google AdMob may collect advertising identifiers and usage data. See the Privacy Policy for details and Google ad settings.
